Q: Set timeout to HTTP response read() method in Python A:

If you're stuck on some Python version 2.6 or lower, one (imperfect, but usable) approach is to do

import socket
socket.setdefaulttimeout(10.0)  # Or whatever

before you start using httplib. The documentation are here, and clearly state that setdefaulttimeout has been available since Python 2.3. Every socket made from the time you do this call, to the time you call the same function again, will use that timeout of 10 seconds. You can use getdefaulttimeout before setting a new timeout, if you want to save the previous timeout (including none), so that you can restore it later (with another setdefaulttimeout).

These functions and idioms are quite useful whenever you need to use some older higher-level library which uses Python sockets, but doesn't give you a good way to set timeouts (of course it's better to use updated higher-level libraries, e.g., the httplib version that comes with 2.6 or the third-party httplib2 in this case, but that's not always feasible, and playing with the default timeout setting can be a good workaround).

Q: Next.js Project Structure A:

Hi! Great question — this is one of the most common points of confusion when moving from the default Next.js template to a real project.

The default structure is intentionally minimal:


app/
├── layout.tsx
├── page.tsx
└── globals.css

But as soon as you add more pages, auth, admin panel, user dashboard, etc., it becomes messy very quickly.
What works well in practice (2026 style)
I personally use a **feature-based + colocated** structure in my open-source Next.js e-commerce project (with App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind, Prisma, shadcn/ui, auth, admin panel, etc.):
https://github.com/Mahdi-Devm/kicks
Here's the high-level structure:

src/
├── app/                        # Only routing + layouts + pages
│   ├── (pages)/
│   ├── admin/                  # Admin dashboard routes
│   ├── auth/                   # Login, register, etc.
│   ├── userpanel/              # User dashboard
│   ├── layout.tsx
│   ├── globals.css
│   └── error.tsx / not-found.tsx
├── core/                       # Shared core logic
│   ├── api-route/              # Server Actions & route handlers
│   ├── components/             # Global & reusable UI
│   │   ├── custom/             # Project-specific blocks (tables, cards, etc.)
│   │   ├── ui/                 # General components
│   │   └── shadcn/ui           # shadcn primitives
│   ├── features/               # Feature folders (group related code)
│   │   ├── admin/
│   │   ├── auth/
│   │   │   ├── components/
│   │   │   └── assets/types/
│   │   ├── main/               # Homepage / core site features
│   │   │   ├── components/
│   │   │   ├── context/
│   │   │   └── utils/
│   │   └── userpanel/
│   ├── lib/                    # Utilities, services, fetchers
│   ├── prisma/                 # Prisma schema & client
│   └── utils/                  # General helpers (cn.ts, formatters, etc.)
└── proxy.ts                    # Optional proxy setup

Quick answers to your questions

1. What is a "component" ?
UI pieces only (things that return JSX). Keep business logic, data fetching, and state management out of them.

  • Global primitives → `core/components/ui/` or `shadcn/ui`
  • Feature-specific → inside `core/features/{feature}/components/`
  • Layout/shared → `core/components/layout/`

2. Where should hooks go?

  • Global hooks (useDebounce, useMedia) → `core/lib/hooks/` or root `hooks/`
  • Feature-specific hooks → inside the feature folder (`core/features/auth/hooks/useAuth.ts`)

3. What is lib/ for?
Shared non-UI utilities: API helpers, formatters, constants, external service wrappers (Cloudinary, Redis, etc.), global hooks if needed.

Why this works
- Keeps `app/` clean (only routing)
- Groups related code by feature (easy to find everything for "auth" or "admin")
- Still simple enough for solo/small teams
- Scales well to 20–50+ pages/features without chaos
- Follows modern Next.js recommendations (route groups, colocated logic)

If your project is very small, you can simplify even more (just `app/ + components/ + lib/`).
But for anything with auth + dashboard + multiple sections, this pattern has worked great in production-like projects.

Feel free to ask about any part (auth, Prisma setup, etc.) — happy to help! 🚀
